system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with prior Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and a gastrostomy tube was admitted to the surgery service for observation after a home accident in which she stepped on and tugged her feeding tube, leading to three days of abdominal pain, increased yellow cloudy drainage, and square-shaped erythema around the dressing. She was kept NPO with tube feeds held, given IV fluids and pain control, and underwent a G-tube contrast study showing the tube tip in the stomach with contrast passing into the small bowel and no extraluminal leak. Tube feeds were restarted and tolerated without nausea or vomiting, and the skin irritation improved with frequent dressing changes; pain persisted mainly at granulation tissue at the tube site but was controlled on oral medication. She was discharged home ambulatory and stable with instructions for ongoing dressing care, PRN pain medication, and surgical follow-up in two weeks for possible tube repositioning if symptoms persist.
problems: Other specified procedures as the cause of abnormal reaction of patient, or of later complication, without mention of misadventure at time of procedure

radiology_notes.text:
HISTORY:  History of bypass surgery with G tube in place, now with
hypoglycemia.  Assess tube placement.

TECHNIQUE:  2 supine AP views of the abdomen were obtained, before after the
administration of oral contrast material through the existing gastric tube.  

COMPARISON:  ___.

FINDINGS:

Initial scout AP view of the abdomen demonstrates a catheter with tip
projecting over the left upper quadrant of the abdomen.  There is mild gaseous
distention of the colon which is also filled with a large amount of stool. 
After the injection of oral contrast material through the existing tube, there
is opacification of the body of the stomach and proximal loops of small bowel,
similar to that seen on the prior exam.  There is no evidence of extraluminal
contrast.

IMPRESSION:

G-tube located within the stomach with no evidence of extraluminal contrast.

HISTORY:  ___ female with refractory hypoglycemia requiring continuous
tube feeds.  Evaluate for passage of contrast.

COMPARISON:  G-tube check dated ___ and plain film of the abdomen
dated ___.

FINDINGS:

Two supine frontal views of the abdomen demonstrate contrast seen throughout
the colon and the rectum.  There is gas in nondistended loops of large and
small bowel without evidence of ileus or obstruction.  The colon contains a
large amount of stool.  The G-tube is seen projecting over the left upper
quadrant.  Suture material from prior gastric surgery is re-identified. 
Visualized osseous structures are unremarkable.  There are multiple
phleboliths in the pelvis.

IMPRESSION:

Interval passage of contrast into the colon and rectum.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. __ from the surgery/bariatric team. I hear you came in because your blood sugar dropped low today. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: This morning I felt jittery and kind of hazy, and my hypoglycemia alarm went off. It said 43. I took sugar pills and it came up, but it scared me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That is scary. Any passing out, seizures, or confusion that didn’t get better after the sugar?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No passing out. I was shaky and not thinking clearly, but it improved after the pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have you had episodes like this since you started tube feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, this is the first time since I started the feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I also see you mentioned more drainage around the G-tube site. What are you noticing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The gauze gets soaked, so I’ve been changing it twice a day. It’s more painful too. I don’t think it’s red, and I don’t have fevers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any new belly pain, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No. Just the tube site hurting and the drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You also had a question about whether the feeds are going into you or refluxing back into the bag by the pump. Tell me what you’re seeing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes it looks like the formula is backing up. I’m worried it’s not actually going in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Tonight we’ll check your blood sugars closely and we’ll do a contrast study through the tube to confirm it’s in the stomach and not leaking. We’ll also examine the skin and tissue around the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is this dangerous? Like could the tube be in the wrong place again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The concern is exactly that—position and leakage—but we can evaluate it quickly with imaging. Right now your exam is reassuring and you don’t have fever or severe abdominal pain, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the low sugar—why would it happen if I’m on feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: After gastric bypass, some people can have hypoglycemia related to how the body handles nutrients and hormones. We’ll make sure you’re safe tonight, and we may involve Endocrinology to guide a more detailed work-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re about to do the G-tube contrast check now. You’ll feel some fluid go through the tube while we take X-ray images.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can feel a little uncomfortable or full, but it shouldn’t be painful. Let us know if you feel sharp pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your tube study is back: the G-tube is located in the stomach and there’s no sign of contrast leaking outside the stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s in the right place?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—proper location and no leak. That makes a major complication much less likely. We’ll continue your tube feeds here and keep checking fingerstick sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Then why is there so much drainage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Often it’s irritation at the skin opening and sometimes overgrowth of granulation tissue—extra healing tissue that can ooze and be tender. We’ll look closely and treat it if that’s what it is.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I examined the site—there is some granulation tissue around the tube. The surrounding skin doesn’t look significantly red or infected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is granulation tissue bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s common and not dangerous by itself, but it can bleed a little, drain, and hurt. We can treat it with silver nitrate to shrink it and use an antibiotic ointment called mupirocin on the area.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Silver nitrate sounds intense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a topical treatment—brief stinging sometimes, but it’s quick. We’ll do it carefully and protect the surrounding skin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today? Any more shakiness overnight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I slept some. No big low sugar episode like yesterday, but I’m still worried it’ll happen again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your fingerstick sugars have been stable so far while on the tube feeds. That’s reassuring. We’re also reviewing possible contributors, including small intestinal bacterial overgrowth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been treated for that before. Are you going to restart antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re restarting metronidazole—Flagyl—500 mg every 8 hours, since bacterial overgrowth may be contributing to the hypoglycemia pattern.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that upset my stomach?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can cause nausea or a metallic taste. We can give ondansetron as needed for nausea. Let us know if you feel worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The tube site still hurts when I move. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: With granulation tissue, tenderness is common. After the silver nitrate treatment and ointment, it should gradually improve. We’ll also keep the dressing clean and dry and change it when saturated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got another abdominal X-ray today to make sure contrast has moved through. It shows the contrast has passed into the colon and rectum, and there’s no obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So my intestines aren’t blocked?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—no ileus or obstruction seen. It also notes a lot of stool in the colon, which can happen, but the key point is there’s passage through.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If my sugars are okay today, why do I need to stay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because you had multiple low readings with symptoms before coming in, and your outpatient endocrinologist asked for a fasting hypoglycemia work-up. That requires close monitoring and timed blood tests while we temporarily stop tube feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fasting sounds like it could make me crash.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s why we do it in the hospital. Nursing will check fingersticks every hour, and we’ll draw labs at specific times. If your sugar drops, we’ll treat it right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Endocrinology reviewed your case and recommends we proceed with the supervised fasting study today. Are you okay moving forward with that plan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous, but yes. What exactly are you testing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: When your glucose gets low, we’ll draw blood for glucose, insulin, C-peptide, and proinsulin, and we’ll also check ammonia. Those results help your endocrinologist understand the cause and guide treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I have to stop the tube feeds completely?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, temporarily, so we can see what your body does without continuous nutrition. We’ll stop them and monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m starting to feel a little shaky. Is my sugar dropping?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We just checked—your fingerstick is still in a safe range right now. Keep telling us about symptoms; we’ll keep the hourly checks going.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My tube site looks less wet today. Is that from the ointment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely, yes—between the silver nitrate shrinking the granulation tissue and the mupirocin plus better dressing care, drainage often improves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been off tube feeds for many hours now. We’re continuing the hourly fingersticks overnight. If you feel sweaty, confused, very shaky, or weak, call right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel shaky and kind of foggy again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your fingerstick is 55. This is the threshold we were watching for. We’re drawing the final set of labs now, then we’ll treat the low sugar immediately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Please don’t let it get worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We won’t. Labs are being drawn now, and we’re giving glucose to bring your level back up. We’ll recheck frequently until you feel normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This morning your sugars have been stable, and you’re alert and feeling better. The fasting work-up is complete, and the results will be visible to your outpatient endocrinologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’re stable, and we want you to make your outpatient appointments. Before you go, we’ll review your medications and tube site care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I keep the tube feeds the same at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You tolerated tube feeds here, and the tube is in the right place. Continue your prescribed tube feeding plan at home, and follow your endocrinologist’s guidance based on the lab results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What do I do if my sugar drops again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use glucose tablets as prescribed for symptoms or low readings. If you have severe symptoms—confusion, inability to take tablets, or you don’t improve—seek emergency care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the tube site—just keep changing the dressing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes: keep it clean and dry, change gauze when saturated, and apply mupirocin ointment to the granulation tissue twice daily as prescribed. Call if you develop spreading redness, fever, or worsening pain.

conversation_lines.text: Do I keep taking the Flagyl?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—metronidazole 500 mg by mouth every 8 hours, as prescribed, for bacterial overgrowth treatment. If you get significant side effects, contact your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on a lot of meds already. Anything new besides those?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: New from this stay are the Flagyl and the mupirocin ointment for the tube site. You’ll also have glucose tablets available for hypoglycemia. The rest of your regimen continues as directed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m anxious about going home after that 55 overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. The drop happened during a supervised fast, which we did on purpose to capture labs. With your usual tube feeds and your rescue glucose tablets, you have a plan. And your endocrinologist will review the results quickly at follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any last questions before discharge paperwork?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No—just please make sure my endocrinologist can see the lab results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The insulin, glucose, C-peptide, proinsulin, ammonia labs from the fasting study are in the system for your outpatient endocrinology team to review. We’ll discharge you home now.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with prior Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and gastrostomy tube for management of post-bypass hypoglycemia was admitted to the surgery/bariatric service after symptomatic hypoglycemia at home (BG 43 improved with glucose tablets) and concern for increased painful drainage around the G-tube. Imaging with contrast through the tube confirmed the G-tube was appropriately positioned in the stomach without extraluminal leak, and tube feeds were continued with no hypoglycemic events on hospital day 1. She was restarted on metronidazole for suspected small intestinal bacterial overgrowth potentially contributing to hypoglycemia, and granulation tissue at the tube site was treated with silver nitrate and mupirocin ointment. At the request of her outpatient endocrinologist, she completed an inpatient supervised fasting hypoglycemia evaluation with hourly fingersticks and timed labs (including glucose, insulin, C-peptide, proinsulin, and ammonia); after ~12 hours off feeds her fingerstick reached 55, labs were drawn, and hypoglycemia was treated. She was discharged home ambulatory and stable with glucose readings 55–110 overnight, prescriptions for metronidazole and mupirocin, and instructions to follow up with endocrinology to review the fasting study results and continue tube-site care.

conversation_lines.text: Is granulation tissue bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s common and not dangerous by itself, but it can bleed a little, drain, and hurt. We can treat it with silver nitrate to shrink it and use an antibiotic ointment called mupirocin on the area.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Silver nitrate sounds intense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a topical treatment—brief stinging sometimes, but it’s quick. We’ll do it carefully and protect the surrounding skin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today? Any more shakiness overnight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I slept some. No big low sugar episode like yesterday, but I’m still worried it’ll happen again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your fingerstick sugars have been stable so far while on the tube feeds. That’s reassuring. We’re also reviewing possible contributors, including small intestinal bacterial overgrowth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been treated for that before. Are you going to restart antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re restarting metronidazole—Flagyl—500 mg every 8 hours, since bacterial overgrowth may be contributing to the hypoglycemia pattern.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that upset my stomach?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can cause nausea or a metallic taste. We can give ondansetron as needed for nausea. Let us know if you feel worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The tube site still hurts when I move. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: With granulation tissue, tenderness is common. After the silver nitrate treatment and ointment, it should gradually improve. We’ll also keep the dressing clean and dry and change it when saturated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got another abdominal X-ray today to make sure contrast has moved through. It shows the contrast has passed into the colon and rectum, and there’s no obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So my intestines aren’t blocked?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—no ileus or obstruction seen. It also notes a lot of stool in the colon, which can happen, but the key point is there’s passage through.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If my sugars are okay today, why do I need to stay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because you had multiple low readings with symptoms before coming in, and your outpatient endocrinologist asked for a fasting hypoglycemia work-up. That requires close monitoring and timed blood tests while we temporarily stop tube feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fasting sounds like it could make me crash.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s why we do it in the hospital. Nursing will check fingersticks every hour, and we’ll draw labs at specific times. If your sugar drops, we’ll treat it right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Endocrinology reviewed your case and recommends we proceed with the supervised fasting study today. Are you okay moving forward with that plan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous, but yes. What exactly are you testing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: When your glucose gets low, we’ll draw blood for glucose, insulin, C-peptide, and proinsulin, and we’ll also check ammonia. Those results help your endocrinologist understand the cause and guide treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I have to stop the tube feeds completely?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, temporarily, so we can see what your body does without continuous nutrition. We’ll stop them and monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m starting to feel a little shaky. Is my sugar dropping?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We just checked—your fingerstick is still in a safe range right now. Keep telling us about symptoms; we’ll keep the hourly checks going.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My tube site looks less wet today. Is that from the ointment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely, yes—between the silver nitrate shrinking the granulation tissue and the mupirocin plus better dressing care, drainage often improves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been off tube feeds for many hours now. We’re continuing the hourly fingersticks overnight. If you feel sweaty, confused, very shaky, or weak, call right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel shaky and kind of foggy again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your fingerstick is 55. This is the threshold we were watching for. We’re drawing the final set of labs now, then we’ll treat the low sugar immediately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Please don’t let it get worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We won’t. Labs are being drawn now, and we’re giving glucose to bring your level back up. We’ll recheck frequently until you feel normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This morning your sugars have been stable, and you’re alert and feeling better. The fasting work-up is complete, and the results will be visible to your outpatient endocrinologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’re stable, and we want you to make your outpatient appointments. Before you go, we’ll review your medications and tube site care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I keep the tube feeds the same at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You tolerated tube feeds here, and the tube is in the right place. Continue your prescribed tube feeding plan at home, and follow your endocrinologist’s guidance based on the lab results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What do I do if my sugar drops again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use glucose tablets as prescribed for symptoms or low readings. If you have severe symptoms—confusion, inability to take tablets, or you don’t improve—seek emergency care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the tube site—just keep changing the dressing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes: keep it clean and dry, change gauze when saturated, and apply mupirocin ointment to the granulation tissue twice daily as prescribed. Call if you develop spreading redness, fever, or worsening pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I keep taking the Flagyl?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—metronidazole 500 mg by mouth every 8 hours, as prescribed, for bacterial overgrowth treatment. If you get significant side effects, contact your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on a lot of meds already. Anything new besides those?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: New from this stay are the Flagyl and the mupirocin ointment for the tube site. You’ll also have glucose tablets available for hypoglycemia. The rest of your regimen continues as directed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m anxious about going home after that 55 overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. The drop happened during a supervised fast, which we did on purpose to capture labs. With your usual tube feeds and your rescue glucose tablets, you have a plan. And your endocrinologist will review the results quickly at follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any last questions before discharge paperwork?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No—just please make sure my endocrinologist can see the lab results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The insulin, glucose, C-peptide, proinsulin, ammonia labs from the fasting study are in the system for your outpatient endocrinology team to review. We’ll discharge you home now.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with prior Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and gastrostomy tube for management of post-bypass hypoglycemia was admitted to the surgery/bariatric service after symptomatic hypoglycemia at home (BG 43 improved with glucose tablets) and concern for increased painful drainage around the G-tube. Imaging with contrast through the tube confirmed the G-tube was appropriately positioned in the stomach without extraluminal leak, and tube feeds were continued with no hypoglycemic events on hospital day 1. She was restarted on metronidazole for suspected small intestinal bacterial overgrowth potentially contributing to hypoglycemia, and granulation tissue at the tube site was treated with silver nitrate and mupirocin ointment. At the request of her outpatient endocrinologist, she completed an inpatient supervised fasting hypoglycemia evaluation with hourly fingersticks and timed labs (including glucose, insulin, C-peptide, proinsulin, and ammonia); after ~12 hours off feeds her fingerstick reached 55, labs were drawn, and hypoglycemia was treated. She was discharged home ambulatory and stable with glucose readings 55–110 overnight, prescriptions for metronidazole and mupirocin, and instructions to follow up with endocrinology to review the fasting study results and continue tube-site care.
